text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

Robusta futures in London rebounded from early lows to end mostly higher. May added $23 to close at $1,720 per tonne, while July closed $18 higher at $1,775 per tonne. Traders fear that the higher levels will inevitably attract scale-up Indonesian and possibly Vietnamese sales, which could put prices under pressure.

Traders said activity was expected to remain thin in the coming days in view of a trade conference in Valencia, Spain, later this week and the approaching long holiday weekend in some European countries.

Arabica futures in New York ended sharply higher as speculators bought heavily amid bullish technical indicators and a fundamental outlook of continued supply tightness. The situation is especially critical as the frost season in Brazil is still ahead and any sign of cold weather could lead to another sharp rise in prices.

Two severe frosts in 1994, one in late June and another in early July, cut Brazil's 1995/96 crop by some 50 per cent and sent futures prices to near 10- year highs. Additionally, traders will keep an eye on second-largest producer Colombia, where some forecasters have cast doubt on the size of the current coffee crop. Current indications are that the 1996/97 (October/September) coffee harvest will fall short of the Colombian Coffee Federation's estimate of about 10.1 mn bags, with most estimates at around 9.6 mn bags, significantly down on last year's figure of 12.9 mn bags.

However, the increase in certified coffee stocks against the exchange could dampen sentiment. The Green Coffee Association data will be released on Thursday and it is possible that stocks could fall or only be up marginally.

May ended 6.65 cents/lb higher at 245.65 cents/lb, while July added 11.75 cents/lb to close at 229.65 cents/lb. The outer months gained between 4.35 and 8.90 cents/lb. However, the prices seen today are not expected to be the peak and further price rices are likely.

BRAZIL - Brazil exported 1.21 mn 60-kg bags of coffee ground and in beans in April, down from 1.54 mn bags exported in March but up on the 543,435 bags exported in the same month in 1996. Brazilian exports so far this year have reached 5.12 mn bags, more than twice the 2.31 mn bags shipped in the first four months of 1996, the Brazilian Federation of Coffee Exporters (Febec) said. Revenue has more than doubled to $862.82 mn from $337.81 mn earned in January/April 1996. The average price per bag rose to $202.73 in April compared with $184.50 in March, Febec said. Of April's total, 1.18 mn bags were arabica coffee, while shipments of conillon reached 37,500 bags.
UNITED STATES - The CSCE reported certified coffee stocks increased by 4,373 bags to 31,292 bags as of May 9. There were 14,310 bags of coffee pending grading, the exchange said.

UNITED STATES - Coffee roastings for the week ended May 3 totalled approximately 285,000 60-kg bags, down from 315,000 bags the previous week and compared with 285,000 bags in the corresponding week one year ago. Cumulative roastings totalled 5.995 mn bags, versus 5.865 mn bags in the same year ago period, Complete Coffee Coverage said.

ITALY - Italy imported 378,224 bags of coffee in December 1996, 1.2 per cent more than was imported the same month the previous year. That brought total imports since the beginning of 1996 up to 5.608 mn bags, 4 per cent more than was imported the previous year.

Main suppliers of green coffee in 1996 were Cameroon (433,300 vs 409,800 bags), Ivory Coast (464,900 vs 425,500 bags), Uganda (331,200 vs 249,600 bags), Zaire (482,000 vs 718,000 bags), Brazil (1.277 vs 1.434 mn bags) and India (447,400 vs 387,400 bags). The country exported 822,500 bags of coffee in 1996, 11 per cent more than was exported the previous year.
